subject: Problems with arrays of matrices on a hierarchical VAR(p) model

messages.author: 268807ff6f08a14c
messages.subject: Problems with arrays of matrices on a hierarchical VAR(p) model
parts:
Hi all,


after finishing the code for a regression model of a time series with autoregressive errors, I would now like to extend this to a VAR. I was thinking about a model of M time series with a lag of P and which includes some exogenous input(s) C, and, besides I would like to make a hierarchical model for J subjects of it. This has all been coded before by Rob Trangucci and Ryan Batt (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/PmGMnqXRD28/AnXr4IVOAgAJ) and I have taken the biggest part of the code from there. Ben Goodrich has also shown a way to code for a correlation matrix for specific subsets of units in a series (see https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/6khmjLtF5I0) which was adopted by Jim Savage. The presented code is thus just my attempt to add all together and make it more general. It also works alright when done with a bunch of for loops generating the coefficients I simulated in an R script, although it is very slow  - as to be expected. The problem I am facing is how to get the model to run efficiently. I have tried to vectorize most of what was easy to do and to apply the nonparametric reparametrization but I am struggling with the access to the matrices especially when there are arrays of matrices. For example, I am trying to estimate z_B as a vector from an array of [P, J, M, M] .

for (p in 1:P){
  for (j in 1:J)
    to_vector(z_beta[p,j]) ~ normal(0,1);
}

This here is not only ugly, it also produces just nans. But even looking in the manual and previous post I can't get my head around how to do this.


The second thing I should optimize is the multinormal distribution. A vectorized form would make the estimation much faster but when I change
 
for(t in 1:(T-P))
    Y_obs[t] ~ multi_normal(mus[t], covar[s_obs[t]]); 

to

Y_obs ~ multi_normal(mus, covar[s_obs]);

it doesn't work and I can't figure out a way to get covariance as a KxK matrix from the KxKxJ array . Of course, another possibility would be to use the Cholesky decomposition but I have not been able to get this running at all. It basically boils down to the question how to include a matrix coming from an array of matrices, I think. So if anyone could help me that would be great. And these are just two bigger issues I see, so if there is more that may be optimized please let me know.
Thanks in advance

Cheers
David

This has all been coded before by Rob Trangucci and Ryan Batt (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/PmGMnqXRD28/AnXr4IVOAgAJ) and I have taken the biggest part of the code from there. Ben Goodrich has also shown a way to code for a correlation matrix for specific subsets of units in a series (see https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/6khmjLtF5I0) which was adopted by Jim Savage. The presented code is thus just my attempt to add all together and make it more general. It also works alright when done with a bunch of for loops generating the coefficients I simulated in an R script, although it is very slow - as to be expected. The problem I am facing is how to get the model to run efficiently. I have tried to vectorize most of what was easy to do and to apply the nonparametric reparametrization but I am struggling with the access to the matrices especially when there are arrays of matrices. For example, I am trying to estimate z_B as a vector from an array of [P, J, M, M] .
>
> for (p in 1:P){
> for (j in 1:J)
> to_vector(z_beta[p,j]) ~ normal(0,1);
> }

You haven't told us what z_beta is. Was z_B meant to be z_beta?
And I don't know what array of P, J, M, M means --- is it a 4D
data structure with sizes P, J, M, and M?

>
> This here is not only ugly, it also produces just nans.

Have you defined z_beta? The sampling notation doesn't sample, it just
increments the log density, so you need to have z_beta defined before
you call the above line.
> But even looking in the manual and previous post I can't get my head around how to do this.
See the manual, section 4.3, Sampling Statements.

>
>
> The second thing I should optimize is the multinormal distribution. A vectorized form would make the estimation much faster but when I change
>
> for(t in 1:(T-P))
> Y_obs[t] ~ multi_normal(mus[t], covar[s_obs[t]]);
>
> to
>
> Y_obs ~ multi_normal(mus, covar[s_obs]);

Look at the available signatures. Y_obs and mus can be
either vectors or arrays of vectors.

> it doesn't work and I can't figure out a way to get covariance as a KxK matrix from the KxKxJ array . Of course, another possibility would be to use the Cholesky decomposition but I have not been able to get this running at all.

We can't help if we don't know what you tried.

The biggest thing you can do for efficiency and stability is
move to a Cholesky factor parameterization.
> It basically boils down to the question how to include a matrix coming from an array of matrices, I think.

Won't work. We don't allow vectorization of the covariance. But
it wouldn't help anyway, even if we did, because the advantage of
vectorization here is only having to factor the matrix once.

What you could do is collect all of the cases with s_obs[t] = k,
which can then share a covariance matrix.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

apologies for not being clear!

So as you were suspecting z_beta is z_B as part of the reparametrization of B.
I just wrote the wrong name. And z_B (as well as B) is four dimensional, that
is J x P x M x M (subject x lag x number of time series x number of time series). 
Is there any way to make this more efficient?

for (p in 1:P){
  for (j in 1:J)

to_vector(z_B[p,j]) ~ normal(0,1);
}


Do you think it makes a big difference?

> What you could do is collect all of the cases with s_obs[t] = k,
which can then share a covariance matrix.

You mean finding time series with a similar amount of data points? I'm afraid
the number of groups is too small for that. Or am I getting you wrong?

Thanks for your advice!
Best,

David


data {
  int<lower=0> T;                     // No. of time periods observed
  int<lower=1> M;                     // No. of variables in y_t
  int<lower=1> P;                     // Lag order
  int<lower=1> J;                    // No. of subjects
  int<lower=1, upper=J>    s[T];        // Subject ID 
  vector[M] Y[T];                     // Obs of state variables
  int nU;                             // No. of exogeneous inputs
  vector[nU] U[T];
}

transformed data {
  vector[M] Y_obs[T-P];                // transforms the data according to the number of lags
  int s_obs[T-P];                    // transforms the index of subjects to match Y_obs
  for (t in 1:(T-P)){
    Y_obs[t] = Y[t + P];
    s_obs[t] = s[t + P];
  }
}

parameters {
  matrix[M,M] Bmu[P];
  matrix<lower=0>[M,M] Bscale[P];
  matrix[M, nU] C[J];                // exogenous inputs
  matrix<lower = 0>[J,M] sigma;        
  corr_matrix[M] Omega_local[J];
  real<lower = 0, upper = 1> rho;
  corr_matrix[M] Omega_global;
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[M, M] B[P,J];                // coefficient for endogeneous inputs
  matrix[M, M] z_B[P,J];            // used for non-centred parametrization
  corr_matrix[M] Omega[J];
for (j in 1:J)
Omega[j] = rho * Omega_global + (1-rho) * Omega_local[j];

for (p in 1:P){
    for (j in 1:J)

B[p,j] = Bmu[p] + Bscale[p] .* z_B[p,j];
  } 
  //print("z_B =", z_B)
}

model {
  matrix[M,M] covar[J];
  vector[M] mus[T-P];
  Omega_global ~ lkj_corr(2);
for (p in 1:P){

to_vector(Bmu[p]) ~ normal(0,1);
    to_vector(Bscale[p]) ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  }
 
  to_vector(sigma) ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  for(j in 1:J) {
    Omega_local[j] ~ lkj_corr(2.0);
    covar[j] = quad_form_diag(Omega[j], sigma[j]);
  }
 
  for (t in 1:(T-P)) {
    mus[t] = C[s[t]] * U[t+P];
for (p in 1:P)
mus[t] = mus[t] + B[p ,s[t]] * Y[t+p-1];

}

  for (p in 1:P){
    for (j in 1:J)
to_vector(z_B[p,j]) ~ normal(0,1);

}
           
  for(t in 1:(T-P))
    Y_obs[t] ~ multi_normal(mus[t], covar[s_obs[t]]);
}
